'''Mark Sapir''' (February 12, 1957&nbsp;- October 8, 2022)<ref name=CV>[https://math.vanderbilt.edu/sapirmv/ftp/vita/Mvs2.pdf Mark Sapir's CV], Department of Mathematics, [[Vanderbilt University]]. Accessed November 4, 2018</ref><ref name=obituary>[https://www.dignitymemorial.com/obituaries/nashville-tn/mark-sapir-10960612 Mark Sapir Obituary]. Accessed October 10, 2022</ref> was a U.S. and Russian mathematician working in [[geometric group theory]], [[semigroup theory]] and combinatorial algebra. He was a Centennial Professor of Mathematics in the Department of Mathematics at [[Vanderbilt University]].

==Education and career==
Sapir received his undergraduate degree in mathematics ([[diploma of higher education]]) from the [[Ural State University]] in [[Yekaterinburg]] (then called Sverdlovsk), [[Russia]], in 1978.<ref name=CV /> He received his PhD in mathematics ([[Candidate of Sciences]]) degree, joint from the [[Ural State University]] and [[Moscow State Pedagogical Institute]] in 1983, with [[Lev Shevrin]] as the advisor.<ref name=CV />

Afterwards Sapir held faculty appointments at the [[Ural State University]], [[:ru:Уральский государственный педагогический университет|Sverdlovsk Pedagogical Institute]], [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]], before coming as a professor of mathematics to [[Vanderbilt University]] in 1997. He was appointed a Centennial Professor of Mathematics at Vanderbilt in 2001.

Sapir gave an invited talk at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Madrid in 2006.<ref>[https://www.mathunion.org/icm-plenary-and-invited-speakers?combine=Sapir ICM Plenary and Invited Speakers], [[International Mathematical Union]]. Accessed November 4, 2018.</ref> He gave an AMS Invited Address at the [[American Mathematical Society]] Sectional Meeting in Huntsville, Alabama in October 2008.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/meetings/sectional/2145_invited.html AMS Sectional Meeting Invited Addresses. 2008 Fall Southeastern Meeting Huntsville, AL, October 24-26, 2008 (Friday – Sunday) Meeting #1044]. [[American Mathematical Society]]. Accessed November 4, 2018.</ref> He gave a plenary talk at the December 2008 Winter Meeting of the [[Canadian Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://cms.math.ca/Events/winter08/abs/Plen.html#ms Plenary lectures], December 2008 Winter Meeting, [[Canadian Mathematical Society]]. Accessed November 4, 2018.</ref> Sapir gave the 33d William J. Spencer Lecture at the [[Kansas State University]] in November 2008.<ref>[https://www.math.ksu.edu/research/lectures/spencer.html William J. Spencer Lectures], Department of Mathematics, [[Kansas State University]]. Accessed November 4, 2018.</ref> He gave the 75th KAM Mathematical Colloquium lecture at the [[Charles University]] in Prague in June 2010.<ref>[https://iuuk.mff.cuni.cz/events/colloquia/ KAM Mathematical Colloquia], Department of Applied Mathematics, [[Charles University]]. Accessed November 4, 2018.</ref>

Sapir became a member of the inaugural class of Fellows of the [[American Mathematical Society]] in 2012.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], [[American Mathematical Society]]. Accessed November 4, 2018.</ref>

Sapir founded the ''[[Journal of Combinatorial Algebra]]'', published by the [[European Mathematical Society]], and served as its founding editor-in-chief starting in 2016.<ref>[http://www.ems-ph.org/journals/editorial.php?jrn=jca Editorial Board], ''Journal of Combinatorial Algebra''. [[European Mathematical Society]]. Accessed November 4, 2018.</ref> He also was an editorial board member for the journals [[Groups, Complexity, Cryptology]] and [[Algebra and Discrete Mathematics]]. His past editorial board positions include [[Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra]], [[Groups, Geometry, and Dynamics]], [[Algebra Universalis]], and [[International Journal of Algebra and Computation]] (as Managing Editor).

A special mathematical conference in honor of Sapir's 60th birthday took place at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]] in May 2017.<ref>[https://faculty.math.illinois.edu/~jsapir2/Sapir60/ CONFERENCE ON GEOMETRIC AND COMBINATORIAL METHODS IN GROUP THEORY. In honor of Mark Sapir's 60th birthday] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181105062239/https://faculty.math.illinois.edu/~jsapir2/Sapir60/ |date=2018-11-05 }} Department of Mathematics, [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]]. Accessed November 4, 2018.</ref>

== Personal life ==
Mark Sapir's elder daughter, [[Jenya Sapir]], is also a mathematician; she was [[Maryam Mirzakhani]]'s first (out of two) students.<ref>{{cite web|title=Jenya Sapir at the Math Genealogy Project|url = https://genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=219599| access-date = Feb 14, 2020}}|</ref> Currently, she is an assistant professor in the Department of Mathematics of [[Binghamton University]].<ref>[http://people.math.binghamton.edu/sapir/Research.html Jenya Sapir's webpage], Department of Mathematics of [[Binghamton University]]. Accessed November 4, 2018.</ref>

Mark Sapir and his wife Olga Sapir became [[United States nationality law|naturalized U.S. citizens]] in July 2003,<ref>[http://www.lexisnexis.com/practiceareas/immigration/pdfs/web433.pdf Sapir vs Aschcroft, Case No. 3:03-0326 (Middle District of Tenn. 2003), Judge Aleta A. Trauger. Order of August 13, 2003.] [[LexisNexis]]. Accessed November 11, 2018.</ref> after suing the [[USCIS|BCIS]] in federal court over a multi-year delay of their citizenship application originally filed in 1999.<ref>Jim Patterson, [https://www.myplainview.com/news/article/Russian-couple-file-lawsuit-over-INS-delay-8939023.php Russian couple file lawsuit over INS delay.] ''[[Plainview Daily Herald]]'', April 24, 2003. Accessed November 11, 2018.</ref>

==Mathematical contributions==

Sapir's early mathematical work concerned mostly [[semigroup theory]].

In [[geometric group theory]] his most well-known and significant results were obtained in two papers published in the [[Annals of Mathematics]] in 2002,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Birget |first1=J.-C. |last2=Ol'shanskii |first2=A. Yu |last3=Rips |first3=E. |last4=Sapir |first4=M. V. |title=Isoperimetric Functions of Groups and Computational Complexity of the Word Problem |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |series=Second Series |date=September 2002 |volume=156 |issue=2 |pages=467 |doi=10.2307/3597196 |jstor=3597196 |mr=1933723|arxiv=math/9811106 |s2cid=14155715 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sapir |first1=Mark V. |last2=Birget |first2=Jean-Camille |last3=Rips |first3=Eliyahu |title=Isoperimetric and Isodiametric Functions of Groups |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |series=Second Series |date=September 2002 |volume=156 |issue=2 |pages=345 |doi=10.2307/3597195 |jstor=3597195 |mr=1933724|arxiv=math/9811105 |s2cid=119728458 }}</ref> the first joint with Jean-Camille Birget and [[Eliyahu Rips]], and the second joint with Birget, Rips and [[Aleksandr Olshansky]]. The first paper provided an essentially complete description of all the possible growth types of [[Dehn function]]s of [[finitely presented group]]s. The second paper proved that a finitely presented group has the [[Word problem for groups|word problem]] solvable in [[NP (complexity)|non-deterministic polynomial time ('''NP''')]] if and only if this group embeds as a [[subgroup]] of a finitely presented group with polynomial Dehn function. A combined featured review of these two papers in [[Mathematical Reviews]] characterized them as ``remarkable foundational results regarding isoperimetric functions of finitely presented groups and their connections with the complexity of the word problem".<ref>Ilya Kapovich (2005) ''[[Mathematical Reviews]]'', {{MR |1933723}} and {{MR |1933724}}.</ref>

Sapir was also known for his work, mostly joint with [[Cornelia Druţu]], on developing the [[asymptotic cone]] approach to the study of [[relatively hyperbolic group]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Druţu |first1=Cornelia |last2=Sapir |first2=Mark |title=Tree-graded spaces and asymptotic cones of groups |journal=[[Topology (journal)|Topology]] |date=September 2005 |volume=44 |issue=5 |pages=959–1058 |doi=10.1016/j.top.2005.03.003 |mr=2153979|doi-access=free |arxiv=math/0405030 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Druţu |first1=Cornelia |last2=Sapir |first2=Mark V. |title=Groups acting on tree-graded spaces and splittings of relatively hyperbolic groups |journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]] |date=February 2008 |volume=217 |issue=3 |pages=1313–1367 |doi=10.1016/j.aim.2007.08.012 |doi-access=free|mr=2383901|s2cid=10461978 }}</ref>

A 2002 paper of Sapir and Olshansky constructed the first known [[finitely presented group|finitely presented]] counter-examples to the [[Von Neumann conjecture]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Olʹshanskii |first1=Alexander Yu. |last2=Sapir |first2=Mark V.  |title=Non-amenable finitely presented torsion-by-cyclic groups |journal=[[Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS]] |issue=96 |year=2002 |pages=43–169 |arxiv=math/0208237 |bibcode=2002math......8237O |mr=1985031}}</ref>

Sapir also introduced, in a 1993 paper with Meakin,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Meakin |first1=John |last2=Sapir |first2=Mark |title=Congruences on free monoids and submonoids of polycyclic monoids |journal=[[Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society, Series A]] |volume=54 |year=1993 |issue=2 |pages=236–253 |doi=10.1017/S1446788700037149 |mr=1200795|doi-access=free }}</ref> the notion of a [[diagram group]], based on finite semigroup presentations. He further developed this notion in subsequent joint papers with Guba.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Guba |first1=Victor |last2=Sapir |first2=Mark |title=Diagram groups |journal=[[Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=1997 |volume=130 |issue=620 |doi=10.1090/memo/0620 |mr=1396957}}</ref> Diagram groups provided a new approach to the study of [[Thompson groups]], which appear as important examples of diagram groups.
